--- title: "FX Prime Brokerage Collateral" subtitle: "A reproducible walkthrough from synthetic FX data to Power BI" author: "Sergio" date: 2026-08-12 format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: false code-tools: true theme: cosmo page-layout: full css: styles.css max-width: 100% syntax-definitions: - dax.xml execute: echo: true output: true warning: false message: false --- # Executive summary This report documents the **FX Prime Brokerage Collateral** project as a reproducible analysis. It walks through the Python pipeline, renders outputs from the generated CSV files, and connects those calculations to the Power BI semantic model and dashboard. The project is synthetic and intended for portfolio demonstration and training. It is not a production margin or collateral engine. ## Setup Start by importing the required modules and loading the generated CSV files. The `find_project_root()` function locates the project folder based on the presence of `data/` and `src/` subfolders. The four datasets are read into a dictionary of DataFrames for later use. The pipeline produces four core datasets: the FX portfolio, counterparty limits, mark-to-market data, and the final MTM collateral report. ::: {#setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from pathlib import Path import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd from IPython.display import display def find_project_root(): candidates = [Path.cwd(), Path.cwd() / "fx-prime-brokerage-collateral"] for candidate in candidates: if (candidate / "data").is_dir() and (candidate / "src").is_dir(): return candidate raise FileNotFoundError("Could not locate the FX collateral project folder") PROJECT_ROOT = find_project_root() DATA_ROOT = PROJECT_ROOT / "data" paths = { "portfolio": DATA_ROOT / "FX-portfolio" / "portfolio.csv", "limits": DATA_ROOT / "Limits" / "limits.csv", "mark_to_market": DATA_ROOT / "Mark-to-market" / "mark_to_market_portfolio.csv", "mtm_report": DATA_ROOT / "Mark-to-market" / "mtm_report.csv", } data = {name: pd.read_csv(path) for name, path in paths.items()} data["mtm_report"]["report_date"] = pd.to_datetime(data["mtm_report"]["report_date"]) data["portfolio"]["report_date"] = pd.to_datetime(data["portfolio"]["report_date"]) ``` ::: ## What the pipeline produces As a summary, the pipeline produces four core datasets: the FX portfolio, counterparty limits, mark-to-market data, and the final collateral report (mtm_report). Each serves a specific purpose in the overall workflow. | Dataset | Grain | Purpose | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | `fx_portfolio` | trade leg and reporting date | FX trades and USD portfolio size | | `limits` | counterparty and as-of date | credit limit, exposure, and availability | | `mark_to_market_portfolio` | trade leg and reporting date | daily FX movement and P&L | | `mtm_report` | reporting date | margin, collateral, and excess/deficit | # 1. Understand the Python pipeline ## Start with the modules Each dataset is generated by a dedicated module, which is called in dependency order by the orchestrator `generate_fx_datasets.py`. | Module | What it does | Output used by | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | `generate_fx_portfolio.py` | creates trade legs, dates, currency pairs, and bank assignments | limits and portfolio MTM | | `generate_limits.py` | creates counterparty credit limits and calculates available capacity | portfolio generation and the Limits page | | `generate_mtm_for_portfolio.py` | simulates daily MTM and P&L for the generated portfolio | collateral report | | `generate_mtm_report.py` | applies margin, collateral, buffer, and deficit/recall rules | dashboard and analysis | | `generate_fx_datasets.py` | calls the stages in order and optionally saves them to PostgreSQL | the complete workflow | The dependency direction is: ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-pipeline %%| fig-cap: "End-to-end FX collateral data pipeline." %%| echo: false flowchart TD A[Portfolio & limit rules] --> B[Generate FX portfolio] B --> C[fx_portfolio.csv] C --> D[Generate limits] C --> E[Generate daily MTM] D --> F[limits.csv] E --> G[mark_to_market_portfolio.csv] G --> H[Generate collateral report] F --> H[Generate collateral report] H --> I[mtm_report.csv] I --> J[Power BI semantic model] J --> K[Dashboard] ``` This ordering matters. 5% of exposure] C[Daily MTM / P&L] --> D[Variation Margin] B --> E[Collateral Required] D --> E E --> F[Compare with
Collateral Posted] F --> G{Excess / Deficit} G -->|Deficit| H[Schedule next-day posting] H --> I[Exposure + buffer] G -->|Surplus| J{Above recall buffer?} J -->|Yes| K[Potential collateral recall] J -->|No| L[No movement] ``` The core logic lives in `src/generate_mtm_report.py`. For each business date: 1. Initial margin is the minimum amount of cash or collateral deposited with a broker to support a leveraged position. For this synthetic model, initial margin is calculated as 5% of active trade exposure and is stored as a negative amount because it represents an obligation to the broker. 2. Variation margin is the aggregated mark-to-market P&L. It keeps its market sign: positive means favourable revaluation and negative means adverse revaluation. 3. Collateral required is the sum of initial margin and variation margin. 4. Posted collateral is the amount already posted by the client to the broker. 5. Excess/deficit compares posted collateral with the positive internal obligation. Negative means more collateral is needed; positive means excess collateral is held. 6. A deficit schedules a next-day posting to reach the exposure plus a buffer (which is normally around \$ 500K). 7. A surplus above the buffer can trigger a collateral recall. ``` python # Simplified calculation from generate_mtm_report.py im_raw = 0.05 * exposure vm_raw = daily_pnl initial_margin = -im_raw variation_margin = vm_raw collateral_required = initial_margin + variation_margin excess_deficit = collateral_required - collateral_posted ``` The current constants are `INITIAL_COLLATERAL = 1_000_000`, `BUFFER = 500_000`, `MOVE_INCREMENT = 10_000`, and `MIN_MOVE = 50_000`. ## The collateral report ::: {#cell-mtm-report-output .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} mtm_report = data["mtm_report"].copy() display(mtm_report.head(10)) ``` ::: {#mtm-report-output .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

height=422} ::: ::: # 3. Power BI documentation ## Project structure The checked-in PBIP project is under `fx-prime-brokerage-collateral/dashboard/`: ``` text dashboard/ ├── fx-prime-brokerage-collateral.pbip ├── fx-prime-brokerage-collateral.Report/ │ └── definition/pages/ └── fx-prime-brokerage-collateral.SemanticModel/ └── definition/ ├── tables/ ├── relationships.tmdl └── model.tmdl ``` The model contains three principal facts (`fx_portfolio`, `limits`, `mtm_report`), supporting dimensions (`dim_date`, `dim_banks`, `dim_currencies`), an FX rates table, and `Measures_Table` for reusable DAX. ## Relationship and filter design The date dimension filters `mtm_report.report_date`, `fx_portfolio.report_date`, and `limits.as_of_date`. Bank and currency dimensions provide reusable slicer paths. The collateral page should therefore use `dim_date[calendar_date]` for time controls rather than placing the fact date directly in every visual. The primary modelling caveat is grain: `mtm_report` is daily, while `fx_portfolio` is trade-leg level. Measures must be used when combining these tables so that a visual does not accidentally sum a daily collateral value once per trade. ## Core DAX measures These are the central measures already present in `Measures_Table.tmdl`: ``` dax Initial Margin = SUM(mtm_report[initial_margin]) Variation Margin = SUM(mtm_report[variation_margin]) Collateral Required = SUM(mtm_report[collateral_required]) Collateral Posted = SUM(mtm_report[collateral_posted]) Excess / Deficit = SUM(mtm_report[excess_deficit]) ``` Because initial margin and collateral required are stored as negative amounts owed to the broker, inverse measures can be useful for visuals where positive means amount required. ``` dax Initial Margin (Inverse) = -1 * SUM(mtm_report[initial_margin]) Collateral Required (Inverse) = -1 * SUM(mtm_report[collateral_required]) ``` ## Previous-day and moving-average patterns The previous-day pattern finds the latest fact date before the current date selected in the date dimension, then evaluates the measure at that date: ``` dax Collateral Posted (Previous Day) = VAR CurrentDate = MAX(dim_date[calendar_date]) VAR PreviousDateWithData = CALCULATE( MAX(mtm_report[report_date]), REMOVEFILTERS(dim_date), dim_date[calendar_date] < CurrentDate ) RETURN CALCULATE( [Collateral Posted], REMOVEFILTERS(dim_date), dim_date[calendar_date] = PreviousDateWithData ) Collateral Posted (Daily Change) = [Collateral Posted] - [Collateral Posted (Previous Day)] ``` For smoothing, the existing model uses a 30-day window: ``` dax IM 30 Day Moving Average = CALCULATE( AVERAGEX( DATESINPERIOD( dim_date[calendar_date], MAX(dim_date[calendar_date]), -30, DAY ), [Initial Margin (Inverse)] ) ) ``` ## Visualisation map | Power BI visual | Fields/measures | Question answered | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | KPI cards | `[Collateral Required (Inverse)]`, `[Collateral Posted]`, `[Excess / Deficit]` | What is the current collateral position? | | Line chart | `dim_date[calendar_date]`, `[Collateral Posted]`, `[Collateral Required (Inverse)]` | How has the requirement moved over time? | | Area or combo chart | `dim_date[calendar_date]`, `[Initial Margin (Inverse)]`, `[Variation Margin]` | What is driving the requirement? | | Column chart | `dim_banks[bank_id]`, `[Counterparty Limits]`, portfolio exposure | Which counterparties consume capacity? | | Detail table | date, bank, currency pair, trade size, margin measures | Which records explain the aggregate? | | Slicers | date, bank, currency, trade type | How can the analyst narrow the review? | The PBIP project contains three principal report pages: **Dashboard**, **Limits**, and **Portfolio**. The Quarto visuals above mirror those analytical roles while remaining independent of Power BI Desktop. ## Practical validation checklist 1. Refresh the source data and confirm the four CSV row counts remain stable on a repeat run. 2. Check that `dim_date` filters all date-bearing facts at the intended grain. 3.
